Cleaning products work in tons of different ways, and some are fascinating! Sorry this response is a month old.

Bleach, or sodium hypochlorite, can be thought of as an oxidizer - it's really just sodium chloride, the salt, with an oxygen stuck in there. Do you think oxygen wants to be stuck in between a salt like that? Heck no! As soon as it has a chance, it'll go do something else instead. Putting bleach on your clothes is basically putting a bunch of reactive oxygen all over your clothes.

Ammonia is another cleaning compound that's also a simple chemical. It's nitrogen that's been fully saturated with hydrogen atoms - nitrogen is happier when it has less than 4 things attached to it, so it will attempt to push hydrogen ions off on other things whenever it gets a chance. This is like the opposite of bleach! Instead of being an acid that pushes oxygen, it's a base that pushes hydrogen.

The opposite-ness of these two chemicals is also why it's so important not to mix them. They react violently with each other - the oxygen and hydrogen group up to make water, which releases a shit ton of energy. Then the ammonium ion grabs the sodium, releasing another shit ton of energy, and the heavy energy barrier forces chlorine to become a gas instead. A corrosive gas that's denser than air and burns your lungs while it suffocates you. Yay!

Many gentler cleaning compounds use these same basic ideas but with something called a buffer solution to help prevent the chemicals from being so reactive. The buffer solution is just some inert salt, but just like loading your car with inert bricks makes it slower these salts make the acid or base less reactive.

More complicated cleaning products use chelating agents - they're kind of like little chemical traps that grab onto particles, then close around them to make them unable to do anything. Febreze is an example of this, any odor particles in the air get wrapped up in ligands and they can't be smelled any more.

The disinfectant you linked didn't come up on my browser, but there are something like a zillion types of disinfectant and they can work by almost any kind of method. Some, like bleach, are strong chemical agents that kill bacteria the same way fire kills people. Others like triclosan or triple quats are specific to the way microbes work and kill them the same way removing a specific part or wire from a car disables the car.

Fun fact: triple quats are bio-accumulative, which means that after they kill a bacteria they leak out of the dead microbe and continue on to kill another one - this is why they are very very bad in your septic tank, and also why wastewater treatment plants hate them.
